adversary.shared_prior: All four lenses lean on the same small citation cluster — the NY governor's office press release/EO text, the Heatmap poll, Good Jobs First's tracker, and the law-firm client alerts (DLA Piper/Davis Polk/Paul Hastings) summarizing the same NY statute. Mean pairwise Jaccard of 0.086 looks low, but that's because each lens cites 1-2 unique 'flavor' sources on top of a shared spine of NY-official and law-firm coverage — the same handful of PR-driven, already-synthesized items (governor's office, three near-identical law-firm alerts, one advocacy tracker) that all pre-package the 'moratorium wave = backlash cascade' narrative. Law-firm client alerts and advocacy trackers are optimized to make regulatory change look sweeping and fast (that's their business model — alerts drive billable engagements, trackers drive donor urgency), so convergence here is partly convergence on a shared marketing/advocacy framing, not four independent readings of primary legislative text.
adversary.counter_case: (1) Base rate for state legislative 'waves': hundreds of bills get introduced every session on every hot-button issue (see: 2021 crypto-mining moratoria, 2018-19 5G/cell-tower moratoria, 2023 short-term-rental bans) and the overwhelming majority die in committee or lapse — 'proposals' and even 'local ordinances' are cheap, reversible, and routinely superseded once a single high-profile economic-development deal is on the table; counting 100+ proposals as a cascade conflates bill introduction (near-zero cost, near-zero signal) with enactment (costly, rare). (2) NY's own law is explicitly temporary (one-year) and carves out DEC/executive-order authority rather than durable statute — that's the signature of a pressure-release valve designed to expire quietly once headlines move on, not a structural regime change; one-year moratoria are a classic legislative stalling tactic, not evidence of a sentiment-to-policy mechanism compressing. (3) Sanders-DeSantis alignment is being read as a powerful cross-partisan wedge, but the more mundane explanation is that both are opportunistically attaching to a local NIMBY fight that long predates AI salience — data-center/warehouse siting opposition (noise, water, tax abatements, land use) has been a live local issue since well before generative AI was a talking point, and re-labeling a land-use backlash as 'AI backlash' is a framing choice by the lenses, not a fact about voter motivation. (4) Selection effect: journalists and trackers (Heatmap, Good Jobs First, law firms) have strong incentives to cover the dramatic cases and ignore the much larger number of jurisdictions where data centers were approved without incident in the same nine months — the denominator (total siting decisions nationally) is never reported, so '100+ moratorium proposals' has no base rate to compare against and may just be normal land-use friction scaled to an industry that's building at record pace.
adversary.weakest_convergence: The 'sentiment-to-legislation lag is compressing to weeks-to-months' claim (ai-public-backlash, echoed by ai-us-policy-direction's 'accelerating growth rate') is the weakest link. It rests on a single anecdote (NH governor moving ~1 month after a grid-operator price signal) generalized into a revised universal lag parameter, and it's the claim every other lens quietly imports without re-deriving — ai-compute-buildout calls the wave 'faster-moving than interconnect queues' and ai-us-policy-direction calls it 'accelerating' largely by citing the same NY timeline. This is a textbook single-case-to-general-rule extrapolation dressed up as a parameter revision, and it's exactly the kind of claim that four lenses reading the same three law-firm alerts would independently launder into 'confirmed, not just suspected.'

librarian.reference_class: State/local moratoria or bans on a specific, newly-controversial land-use/infrastructure type, enacted in response to a fast-rising, geographically diffuse public grievance (e.g., fracking bans/moratoria 2010-2014, cell tower/5G siting moratoria, LNG export terminal and pipeline local bans, big-box/Walmart siting bans 1990s-2000s, casino and landfill siting moratoria, short-term rental bans post-2015)
librarian.class_size: roughly 15-25 comparable multi-state infrastructure-siting backlash waves since 1990, each spawning dozens to hundreds of local/state proposals within 1-2 years of the grievance becoming salient
librarian.base_rate: in this class, the great majority of proposals never become enacted, binding law (most die in committee, get watered down to studies/setbacks, or are preempted/struck down); a minority (roughly 1-in-4 to 1-in-3) of jurisdictions that propose a moratorium actually enact one, and enacted moratoria are usually temporary, narrow, or later relaxed once the industry offers concessions (tax revenue sharing, price caps, remote siting) or the acute cost driver eases; full sector-wide multi-state bans that stick for years are rare (fracking bans in NY/VT persisted, but most fracking-state proposals didn't ban outright, and most cell-tower/5G moratoria were struck down or expired)
librarian.outside_view: Base rates say expect a fast proposal wave to keep growing in count for another 6-18 months, then plateau and fragment as industry buys off the sharpest grievance (electricity price relief, tax-sharing, remote siting) state by state; expect maybe 3-8 of the 100+ proposals to become real enacted law in the next year, not a cascade of 15+, and expect the coalition (Sanders-DeSantis) to fracture once concessions target each side's specific complaint, since cross-partisan alliances in this class are typically united by convenience rather than shared diagnosis and rarely survive contact with sector lobbying.
librarian.disagreement: The lenses treat the current velocity (100+ proposals in under a year, NY-to-law in ~6 weeks) as evidence the sentiment-to-law lag is structurally compressing for this issue; the outside view treats that velocity as normal early-wave enthusiasm that historically decelerates once industry concessions peel off the coalition, making the lenses' 15+ enactments and multi-state-law expectations likely overconfident on both count and durability.

occam.boring_explanation: Electricity bills went up, people noticed, and politicians in an election year did the easy popular thing. Data centers are large, visible, unpopular new industrial neighbors (noise, water, land, grid strain) that make an easy local target regardless of AI hype — this is standard NIMBY-plus-utility-rate politics, the same pattern seen historically with power plants, landfills, and cell towers. Sanders and DeSantis agreeing on 'my constituents' bills went up, blame the nearby industrial facility' requires zero coordination — it's two populists independently reading the same polling.
occam.complexity_saved: Drops: a compressing 'sentiment-to-legislation lag' constant requiring revision, a deliberate federal EO 'carve-out' strategy, an emergent multi-state institutional taxonomy (PUC vs DEC vs local-control models), a stacking-constraint theory of capex risk, and any claim that this is a coordinated or structurally novel backlash mechanism rather than default legislative reflex to a cost-of-living complaint. None of the four lenses' machinery is needed to explain politicians responding to angry ratepayers within one legislative cycle — that's how legislatures normally work.
occam.where_boring_loses: If moratorium language explicitly targets AI/safety framing rather than electricity costs or land use in most enacted statutes (not just NY), or if the moratoriums keep spreading in states with flat/falling electricity prices, that would mean this is about AI specifically rather than ordinary utility-rate NIMBYism wearing an AI costume.

Both flag the Sanders-DeSantis coalition as real but fragile/asymmetric — united by opposite grievances (grid price vs. tax/justice framing) rather than a shared diagnosis, which bears on durability even though both treat the current wave as significant.

Both center NY's executive-order mechanism (Governor + DEC) rather than the legislature or PUC as the operative institutional lever, and both note it deliberately avoids/predates a federal collision rather than triggering one.

tensions.sides: Lens models say the sentiment-to-legislation lag is structurally compressing to weeks-to-months for issues with quantifiable individual harm plus a credible third-party validator, and expect 15+ enactments by mid-2027; the outside view says this is normal early-wave proposal enthusiasm (bill introduction is cheap) that historically decelerates once industry buys off the sharpest grievance, predicting only 3-8 real enactments.
tensions.decider: The actual enacted (not proposed) count of binding, still-in-force data-center moratorium statutes as of 2027-06-30 — above ~10-15 favors the compression thesis, below 10 favors the base rate.

tensions.sides: ai-rising-powers reads NY's EO + state fragmentation (NY/DEC vs OK/PUC vs SD/localism) as evidence of a novel, AI-specific institutional realignment in siting authority; the simplicity judge says this is boring rate-shock NIMBYism with no new mechanism, just states reaching for whatever existing institutional lever (governor, PUC, or local council) was already closest at hand.
tensions.decider: Whether enacted statutes explicitly cite AI/safety framing versus electricity-cost/land-use framing — and whether the same institutional pattern (PUC, DEC, or local control) recurs as a deliberate template in the next 2-3 states, versus each state independently reusing whatever generic siting tool it already had.

tensions.sides: ai-us-policy-direction reads the Dec 2025 federal preemption EO's data-center carve-out as a deliberate strategic concession that lowers friction for state moratoria; the devil's advocate implies simpler explanations (ordinary land-use politics, no coordination) are sufficient and don't require reading strategic intent into the EO's scope.
tensions.decider: Whether DOJ's Litigation Task Force attempts a Dormant Commerce Clause challenge to state moratoria within the carve-out's scope — an actual legal challenge would confirm the carve-out was contested terrain, not settled indifference.

crossed.insight: Combining the two reveals that the 'stacking constraint' on capex isn't uniform across states — because siting authority is fragmenting into at least three institutional models (NY governor/DEC, OK PUC, SD local-statute), the capex risk to any given hyperscaler project depends on which state-specific chokepoint applies, meaning national capex-at-risk estimates (30-50%) likely mask sharp state-by-state variance in how fast a moratorium can be reversed or negotiated around.

The federal EO's deliberate carve-out for data-center moratoria, combined with backlash's finding that this issue compresses the sentiment-to-law lag unusually fast, implies the administration may have inadvertently ceded the single fastest-moving state AI-adjacent policy lane to bipartisan populism — a federal preemption move here would now face a harder, faster-hardening target than when the carve-out was drafted.

load_bearing.why: Every other lens's read of speed, durability, and institutional response is downstream of whether the sentiment-to-law lag is actually compressing — if that's wrong (per the base-rate outside view), the buildout, rising-powers, and policy-direction readings all overstate structural novelty rather than describing an ordinary, decelerating NIMBY wave.

synthesis.da_response: Concede to BASE-RATE LIBRARIAN: the 15+ enactment expectations from backlash/policy-direction are likely overconfident — added a null joint_claim (<10 enacted) at 0.5 confidence to hedge this directly. Concede to DEVIL'S ADVOCATE on shared-source risk: the four lenses do lean on the same NY-official/law-firm spine, so 'confirmed, not suspected' language in the lens reads should be downgraded to 'suggestive, pending enactment data.' Rebut SIMPLICITY JUDGE's full reduction: even if the underlying driver is ordinary rate-shock NIMBYism, ai-rising-powers' finding of genuinely divergent institutional responses (DEC vs PUC vs local-statute) across only three states in weeks is a real structural detail the boring story doesn't predict or explain — that variance is worth tracking regardless of motive. Rebut on cross-partisan alignment: even if Sanders-DeSantis convergence needs no coordination, its existence still lowers future federal preemption's political cost, which is a real, checkable claim independent of whether the underlying grievance is 'about AI' or not.
synthesis.honest_note: The whole ensemble under-weights the base rate that most legislative waves die in committee; the joint_claims lean on the same shared citation cluster (NY press releases, three near-identical law-firm alerts, one advocacy tracker) that the devil's advocate flagged, so 'four lenses agree' is closer to 'four lenses read the same three sources' than independent confirmation.
